It's not about using our experience to paint; it's about channeling the divine when we do so. The same applies when we sing or tell stories—we are merely a portal for the divine to communicate. When you speak, you're channeling the vine; writing, however, is seen as counterfeiting the divine. For them, stopping talking was akin to singing, and capturing music in written form would corrupt it.

The cave paintings contain symbols rather than pictures. Genevie von Piter, a Canadian archaeologist, spent decades cataloging these symbols across various European caves. These symbols are crucial; they represent a writing system but were not used for writing because writing is viewed as corrupting the natural world.

Everything should be a communal experience—singing, talking, and painting together. Writing, on the other hand, is solitary, which explains why early humans chose not to write despite having the capacity from the beginning. This decision was conscious and considered a corruption of the natural world.

The symbols in art are necessary for expressing certain abstractions like energy or life force cycles. They also help visualize the spirit world's language, storing memories and commemorating events on stones. These actions bring beauty and imagination to the world, celebrating the divine, and helping us understand how the spirit world works within our reality.

Lastly, these symbols tell stories about who we are, combining imagination to create society, belonging, and community.
